base_method_text.title:
Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model
  Scaling Laws
base_method_text.summary:
Large language model (LLM) scaling laws are empirical formulas that estimate
changes in model quality as a result of increasing parameter count and training
data. However, these formulas, including the popular Deepmind Chinchilla
scaling laws, neglect to include the cost of inference. We modify the
Chinchilla scaling laws to calculate the optimal LLM parameter count and
pre-training data size to train and deploy a model of a given quality and
inference demand. We conduct our analysis both in terms of a compute budget and
real-world costs and find that LLM researchers expecting reasonably large
inference demand (~1B requests) should train models smaller and longer than
Chinchilla-optimal. Furthermore, we train 47 models of varying sizes and
parameter counts to validate our formula and find that model quality continues
to improve as we scale tokens per parameter to extreme ranges (up to 10,000).
Finally, we ablate the procedure used to fit the Chinchilla scaling law
coefficients and find that developing scaling laws only from data collected at
typical token/parameter ratios overestimates the impact of additional tokens at
these extreme ranges.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper addresses the limitations of existing LLM scaling laws, such as the Chinchilla scaling laws, which do not account for inference costs. It modifies these laws to determine the optimal model size and training data size considering both training and inference demands. The study validates the modified scaling laws through extensive experiments and ablates the curve fitting procedure, revealing that existing laws overestimate the impact of additional training data in extreme data regimes.
base_method_text.methodology: The research modifies the Chinchilla scaling laws by incorporating inference costs into the optimization problem. It uses pre-training cross-entropy loss as a proxy for model quality and FLOPs as the unit of computational cost. The optimization problem is solved computationally using the Newton root-finding method. Real-world cost optimality is estimated by accounting for hardware utilization and costs.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The study involves training 47 models with the MPT architecture, ranging from 150M to 6B parameters, with data budgets from 10 to 10,000 tokens per parameter. The models are evaluated on a version of the open-source Evaluation Gauntlet, which includes tasks in world knowledge, commonsense reasoning, reading comprehension, language understanding, and symbolic problem-solving.
base_method_text.limitations: The analysis assumes that LLM practitioners can estimate inference demand prior to training. The experimental data is limited in terms of model size (up to 6B parameters) and the number of training runs (47 vs. 400 in the Chinchilla paper). The real-world cost estimation model simplifies hardware utilization and costs, leaving aside latency requirements and assuming MFU and cost per FLOP do not depend on model size, configuration, or sequence length.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring scaling laws beyond 10,000 tokens per parameter and at larger model sizes. Further work is needed to develop scaling laws that apply precisely at a wide range of ratios and to understand the limits of scaling law extrapolation. Additional research is also suggested to explore the minimum data required to accurately fit scaling laws coefficients.

add_method_texts.title: Scaling Inference-Efficient Language Models
add_method_texts.summary:
Scaling laws are powerful tools to predict the performance of large language
models. However, current scaling laws fall short of accounting for inference
costs. In this work, we first show that model architecture affects inference
latency, where models of the same size can have up to 3.5x difference in
latency. To tackle this challenge, we modify the Chinchilla scaling laws to
co-optimize the model parameter count, the number of training tokens, and the
model architecture. Due to the reason that models of similar training loss
exhibit gaps in downstream evaluation, we also propose a novel method to train
inference-efficient models based on the revised scaling laws. We perform
extensive empirical studies to fit and evaluate our inference-aware scaling
laws. We vary model parameters from 80M to 1B, training tokens from 1.6B to
30B, and model shapes, training a total of 63 models. Guided by our
inference-efficient scaling law and model selection method, we release the
Morph-1B model, which improves inference latency by 1.8x while maintaining
accuracy on downstream tasks compared to open-source models, pushing the Pareto
frontier of accuracy-latency tradeoff.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper addresses the problem of inference costs being disregarded by current scaling laws for large language models (LLMs). It introduces inference-efficient scaling laws that co-optimize model parameter count, training tokens, and model architecture. A novel method is proposed to train inference-efficient models based on the revised scaling laws, and the Morph-1B model is released, demonstrating improved inference latency while maintaining accuracy.
add_method_texts.methodology: The research modifies the Chinchilla scaling laws to incorporate model architecture considerations. It involves training multiple models with varying parameters, tokens, and shapes, then fitting the inference-efficient scaling laws using the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. A novel method is developed to rank model architectural choices based on loss predictions from scaling laws.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: Experiments involved training over 60 models ranging from 80M to 1B parameters and 1.6B to 30B tokens. Models were evaluated on 11 downstream tasks used by Open-LM, and inference latency was measured on a single NVIDIA Ampere 40GB A100 GPU. The DCLM-Baseline dataset was used for training, and zero-shot evaluation was performed using LLM-foundry.
add_method_texts.limitations: The training was not scaled to include 7B models due to resource limitations. The scaling laws are based on specific model architectures and may not generalize to all architectures. The study also acknowledges that recently developed inference systems could introduce new trade-offs.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: Future research directions include scaling training to larger models (e.g., 7B), exploring the impact of new inference systems and architectural optimizations (like MQA, GQA, MLA) on the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff, and further refining the scaling laws to account for these factors. The work also calls for designing language models with inference efficiency as a primary consideration.
